content.thinking:
I need to avoid inventing specific figures and use placeholders instead. I'm tracing the root-cause chain: shoppers' spend totals were wrong per the cited evidence, and digging into why points to the monthly-spend feature being enabled around a certain time, with the oldest affected purchase matching that onset — suggesting a likely candidate cause tied to that rollout.

I don't have record evidence for the exact defect in the new computation path, so I should state that the flag causing the issue is the leading hypothesis but remains unverified. I also need to flag contributing factors — the infrequent integrity-check cadence that let the fault run undetected, and the lack of reconciliation validation or gradual rollout — and translate these into action items covering detection, prevention, and repair of already-corrupted totals.

For the executive summary, I should avoid writing specific numbers directly and instead reference them as placeholders, noting the duration of impact, scope of affected shoppers, the shortfall amount, and that Argus recommended reverting the flag but didn't act automatically while a draft fix was proposed. For lessons learned, I'm noting that the integrity check and Argus's correlation with the change log worked well, while detection speed and Argus's inability to act autonomously were weaknesses — and that the change log being timestamped was the key piece of evidence that made correlation possible at all.

Now I'm building out the causal chain, mapping each step to its evidence citations: the mismatch between shopper totals and purchases ties to one alert source, the timing and scope of the bad writes tie to several metrics and trace sources, and the root cause traces back to when the flag was switched on according to the change-history record.

I'll frame the final step as the likely root cause—that the flag enabled a new spend-total path producing incorrect writes—while noting this hasn't been confirmed by an actual trial, since the record doesn't directly expose the defect itself.

action_items.item: Run the spend-integrity check far more often than every {A5} days, or run it continuously on newly written totals, and alert when any total does not reconcile.
Require a reconciliation check on spend totals before and during any flag rollout that changes how totals are computed. Roll out in stages and stop if totals diverge.
Recompute and repair every shopper total written since {began} from the purchases behind it. Re-run the integrity check afterwards to confirm all totals reconcile.
Give Argus a cheap way to verify a flag rollback, such as a reconciliation probe on newly written totals, so it can take the action itself and confirm the result.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' spend totals did not reconcile with their purchases. The integrity check found {A1} of {A2} totals wrong, the widest short by {A3}.

The totals have been wrong since about {began}. The oldest affected purchase was recorded at {A4}. Per-minute metrics showed no operational departure, so the corruption was silent and no error-rate alert could fire.

The monthly-spend-feature flag was switched on at {P1.1}, just before the oldest bad purchase, and was still on in the recent logs. It was the only production change read and the only recent flag change.

The flag enabled a new spend-total computation path that writes totals that do not match the purchases. The record does not show the defect in that path, and nothing was tried to confirm it. Argus recommended putting the flag back and proposed a draft fix.

contributing_factors.factor: Wrong totals were only found by a check that runs every {A5} days, so the fault could run for up to {duration} before anyone knew. No metric or log line showed it.
The flag was switched on for all shoppers with no reconciliation check on the new path. Nothing compared the new totals with the purchases behind them at rollout.
Totals already written wrongly during the incident stay wrong after the flag is put back or the code is fixed.
Argus could not tell within its waiting time whether putting the flag back worked, so it did not act. The fault carried on until a person acted.

input.executive_summary: Shoppers' spend totals stopped matching their purchases. A periodic integrity check found that {A1} of {A2} totals checked were wrong, the widest by {A3}. The fault began at about {began} and was still present when the last metrics were read, so it lasted at least {duration}. Pages stayed fast and error-free, so nothing flagged it until the check ran. Argus held the incident for {held}. It traced the start to a feature flag switched on minutes before the first bad purchase. It recommended switching the flag back instead of doing so itself, because it could not confirm within its waiting time that the action had worked. It also opened a draft pull request with a proposed fix. Totals already written wrongly are not repaired by switching the flag back.

went_well: Argus tied the first wrong purchase to a flag change made minutes earlier and ranked it as the leading cause.
Argus raised a draft fix and a clear recommendation for a person within moments of the alert.
went_wrong: The corruption was invisible to operational metrics and went undetected until the periodic check ran.
With no metrics from before the onset, the error rate could not be measured against a calm baseline.
The recommended rollback was not taken, so the fault was still present when the incident closed.

input.root_cause: Switching on the monthly-spend-feature flag at {P1.1} enabled a new spend-total path that writes totals which do not reconcile with the purchases behind them. The record shows the timing match and that the flag was on, but the defect inside that path is not identified. Putting the flag back was recommended and never tried, so the link is not confirmed.
